claim: TRPV1 channel is activated by heat.
source: The Transient Receptor Potential Vanilloid 1 (TRPV) channel is activated by an array of stimuli, including heat and vanilloid compounds.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract as a known property of TRPV1.

claim: TRPV1 channel is activated by vanilloid compounds.
source: The Transient Receptor Potential Vanilloid 1 (TRPV) channel is activated by an array of stimuli, including heat and vanilloid compounds.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract as a known property of TRPV1.

claim: TRPV2 is activated by heat.
source: The TRPV1 homologues TRPV2 and TRPV3 are also activated by heat, but sensitivity to vanilloids and many other agonists is not conserved among TRPV subfamily members.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract.

claim: TRPV3 is activated by heat.

claim: Four mutations in TRPV2 are sufficient to render the channel sensitive to resiniferatoxin (RTx).
source: It was recently discovered that four mutations in TRPV2 are sufficient to render the channel sensitive to the TRPV1-specific vanilloid agonist resiniferatoxin (RTx).
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Mutation of six residues in TRPV3 corresponding to the vanilloid site in TRPV1 is sufficient to engineer RTx binding.
source: Here, we show that mutation of six residues in TRPV3 corresponding to the vanilloid site in TRPV1 is sufficient to engineer RTx binding.
evidence: Main finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through experimental data in the results section.

claim: Robust activation of TRPV3 by RTx requires facilitation of channel opening by introducing mutations in the pore.
source: However, robust activation of TRPV3 by RTx requires facilitation of channel opening by introducing mutations in the pore, temperatures > 30°C, or sensitization with another agonist.
evidence: Main finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through experimental data in the results section.

claim: Robust activation of TRPV3 by RTx requires temperatures > 30°C.
source: However, robust activation of TRPV3 by RTx requires facilitation of channel opening by introducing mutations in the pore, temperatures > 30°C, or sensitization with another agonist.
evidence: Main finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through experimental data in the results section.

claim: Robust activation of TRPV3 by RTx requires sensitization with another agonist.
source: However, robust activation of TRPV3 by RTx requires facilitation of channel opening by introducing mutations in the pore, temperatures > 30°C, or sensitization with another agonist.
evidence: Main finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through experimental data in the results section.

claim: The energetics of channel activation can determine the apparent sensitivity to a stimulus.
source: Our results demonstrate that the energetics of channel activation can determine the apparent sensitivity to a stimulus and suggest that allosteric pathways for activation are conserved in the TRPV family.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Allosteric pathways for activation are conserved in the TRPV family.
source: Our results demonstrate that the energetics of channel activation can determine the apparent sensitivity to a stimulus and suggest that allosteric pathways for activation are conserved in the TRPV family.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: TRP channels are tetramers.
source: Structurally, TRP channels are tetramers, with each subunit containing six transmembrane helices (S1-S6); the region encompassing the S5 through S6 helices forms the central ion-conducting pore, and the S1-S4 helices of each subunit form voltage sensor-like domains located peripherally in a domain-swapped arrangement (Madej and Ziegler, 2018).
evidence: Stated as established structural knowledge with citation.

claim: Each TRP channel subunit contains six transmembrane helices (S1-S6).
source: Structurally, TRP channels are tetramers, with each subunit containing six transmembrane helices (S1-S6); the region encompassing the S5 through S6 helices forms the central ion-conducting pore, and the S1-S4 helices of each subunit form voltage sensor-like domains located peripherally in a domain-swapped arrangement (Madej and Ziegler, 2018).
evidence: Stated as established structural knowledge with citation.

evidence: Stated as established structural knowledge with citation.

claim: TRPV1 and TRPV2 share 48.4% sequence identity.
source: This is well exemplified by TRPV1 and its closest homologue, TRPV2 (48.4% of sequence identity).
evidence: Stated directly in the introduction.

claim: TRPV1 is an integrator of pain-producing stimuli in nociceptors.
source: TRPV1, an integrator of pain-producing stimuli in nociceptors (Moore et al., 2018), is the only member of the TRPV (vanilloid) subfamily of TRP channels that can be activated by vanilloid compounds (Caterina et al., 1997; Jordt and Julius, 2002), cysteine-reactive molecules (Salazar et al., 2008), and some agonists that directly interact with the extracellular face of the pore domain, such as protons (Tominaga et al., 1998; Jordt et al., 2000) and the double-knot toxin (DkTx) from tarantula venom (Bohlen et al., 2010; Cao et al., 2013; Bae et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated with citation to support the claim.

claim: TRPV1 is the only member of the TRPV subfamily that can be activated by vanilloid compounds.
source: TRPV1, an integrator of pain-producing stimuli in nociceptors (Moore et al., 2018), is the only member of the TRPV (vanilloid) subfamily of TRP channels that can be activated by vanilloid compounds (Caterina et al., 1997; Jordt and Julius, 2002), cysteine-reactive molecules (Salazar et al., 2008), and some agonists that directly interact with the extracellular face of the pore domain, such as protons (Tominaga et al., 1998; Jordt et al., 2000) and the double-knot toxin (DkTx) from tarantula venom (Bohlen et al., 2010; Cao et al., 2013; Bae et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: TRPV2 is activated by heat.
source: In contrast, TRPV2 is activated by very few known stimuli, including heat (Caterina et al., 1999; Yao et al., 2011), the non-selective channel modulator 2-aminoethoxydiphenyl borate (2-APB) (Hu et al., 2004) and cannabinoid compounds (Qin et al., 2008), all of which also influence the activity of TRPV1 (Hu et al., 2004; Qin et al., 2008).
evidence: Stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: TRPV2 is activated by 2-aminoethoxydiphenyl borate (2-APB).
source: In contrast, TRPV2 is activated by very few known stimuli, including heat (Caterina et al., 1999; Yao et al., 2011), the non-selective channel modulator 2-aminoethoxydiphenyl borate (2-APB) (Hu et al., 2004) and cannabinoid compounds (Qin et al., 2008), all of which also influence the activity of TRPV1 (Hu et al., 2004; Qin et al., 2008).

evidence: Stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: RTx binds to the same site between the S1-S4 domains and the pore domain in both TRPV1 and TRPV2-4M.
source: Indeed, structural studies have confirmed that RTx binds to the same site between the S1-S4 domains and the pore domain in both TRPV1 (Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016) and TRPV2-4M (Zubcevic et al., 2018b) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Stated with citations to structural studies and reference to a figure showing the binding site.

claim: TRPV3 shares 42% sequence identity with TRPV1.
source: In the present study, we explored whether vanilloid sensitivity could be engineered into the TRPV3 channel, which shares 42% sequence identity with TRPV1.
evidence: Stated directly in the introduction.

claim: TRPV3 is expressed primarily in mammalian keratinocytes.
source: TRPV3 is expressed primarily in mammalian keratinocytes, where it is required for the formation of the skin barrier (Cheng et al., 2010), and mutations in the channel can lead to skin diseases such as Olmsted Syndrome (Lin et al., 2012; Zhi et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated with citation to support the claim.

claim: TRPV3 is required for the formation of the skin barrier.
source: TRPV3 is expressed primarily in mammalian keratinocytes, where it is required for the formation of the skin barrier (Cheng et al., 2010), and mutations in the channel can lead to skin diseases such as Olmsted Syndrome (Lin et al., 2012; Zhi et al., 2016).

evidence: Stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: TRPV3 is a polymodal detector of warm temperatures.
source: TRPV3 is a polymodal detector of warm temperatures (Peier et al., 2002; Smith et al., 2002; Xu et al., 2002), chemicals such as 2-APB (Chung et al., 2004; Hu et al., 2004) and multiple natural products such as camphor, eugenol and thymol (Xu et al., 2006; Vogt-Eisele et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated with citations to support the claim.

evidence: Stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: TRPV3-4M was not activated by 100 nM RTx at room temperature.
source: Whereas TRPV2-4M displayed robust responses to RTx (Figure 1C), as we showed previously (Zhang et al., 2016), TRPV3-4M was activated by 2-APB but not by 100 nM RTx (Figure 1D), a concentration that is saturating for both TRPV1 and TRPV2-4M (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 1D and described in text.

claim: TRPV3-4M was activated by 2-APB.
source: Whereas TRPV2-4M displayed robust responses to RTx (Figure 1C), as we showed previously (Zhang et al., 2016), TRPV3-4M was activated by 2-APB but not by 100 nM RTx (Figure 1D), a concentration that is saturating for both TRPV1 and TRPV2-4M (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 1D and described in text.

claim: 100 nM RTx is a saturating concentration for TRPV1.
source: Whereas TRPV2-4M displayed robust responses to RTx (Figure 1C), as we showed previously (Zhang et al., 2016), TRPV3-4M was activated by 2-APB but not by 100 nM RTx (Figure 1D), a concentration that is saturating for both TRPV1 and TRPV2-4M (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated with citation to previous work.

claim: 100 nM RTx is a saturating concentration for TRPV2-4M.
source: Whereas TRPV2-4M displayed robust responses to RTx (Figure 1C), as we showed previously (Zhang et al., 2016), TRPV3-4M was activated by 2-APB but not by 100 nM RTx (Figure 1D), a concentration that is saturating for both TRPV1 and TRPV2-4M (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated with citation to previous work.

claim: TRPV3-6M remained insensitive to RTx at room temperature.
source: We therefore mutated these two additional positions in TRPV3-4M to the corresponding residues in TRPV1 to generate TRPV3-6M, and found that the construct remained insensitive to RTx, although it retained robust responses to 2-APB (Figure 1E).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 1E and described in text.

claim: TRPV3-6M retained robust responses to 2-APB.
source: We therefore mutated these two additional positions in TRPV3-4M to the corresponding residues in TRPV1 to generate TRPV3-6M, and found that the construct remained insensitive to RTx, although it retained robust responses to 2-APB (Figure 1E).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 1E and described in text.

claim: TRPV3-6M/V2P chimera was robustly activated by RTx.
source: Remarkably, the resulting chimera was robustly activated by RTx and readily blocked by RR (Figure 1F), indicating that the pore domain of TRPV2 contains determinants that are important for RTx-activation.
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 1F and described in text.

claim: The pore domain of TRPV2 contains determinants that are important for RTx-activation.
source: Remarkably, the resulting chimera was robustly activated by RTx and readily blocked by RR (Figure 1F), indicating that the pore domain of TRPV2 contains determinants that are important for RTx-activation.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental result that TRPV3-6M/V2P was activated by RTx.

claim: TRPV3-4M/V2P could be activated by 2-APB but not by RTx.
source: We also found that the two additional residues in the vanilloid pocket differing between TRPV3-4M and TRPV3-6M were necessary for RTx activation, since we transferred the pore domain of TRPV2 into TRPV3-4M to generate TRPV3-4M/V2P (Figure 1A), and found that the resulting chimera could be activated by 2-APB but not by RTx (Figure 1G).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 1G and described in text.

claim: The two additional residues in the vanilloid pocket differing between TRPV3-4M and TRPV3-6M are necessary for RTx activation.
source: We also found that the two additional residues in the vanilloid pocket differing between TRPV3-4M and TRPV3-6M were necessary for RTx activation, since we transferred the pore domain of TRPV2 into TRPV3-4M to generate TRPV3-4M/V2P (Figure 1A), and found that the resulting chimera could be activated by 2-APB but not by RTx (Figure 1G).
evidence: Inference drawn from comparing TRPV3-4M/V2P and TRPV3-6M/V2P results.

claim: Five individual mutations in the pore domain of TRPV3-6M resulted in constructs with robust RTx-activated currents (V587L, A606V, F625L, F656I, F666Y).
source: We identified five positions that when individually mutated resulted in constructs with robust RTx-activated currents that were very similar in magnitude to those elicited by 2-APB (V587L, A606V, F625L, F656I, F666Y; Figure 2B,C, dark blue).
evidence: Experimental results shown in Figure 2B,C and described in text.

claim: Five individual mutations in the pore domain of TRPV3-6M exhibited detectable but smaller responses to RTx (I595L, K611D, L635F, L639M, Y650F).
source: In addition, five constructs with individual mutations at additional positions exhibited detectable responses to RTx (I595L, K611D, L635F, L639M, Y650F; Figure 2B–D, light blue, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1) that were, however, smaller than the responses to 2-APB in those same constructs.
evidence: Experimental results shown in Figure 2B-D and described in text.

claim: Eleven individual residue substitutions in the pore domain resulted in RTx-insensitive constructs that were still activated by 2-APB (L596V, L599F, S613K, D618P, S620E, I644F, Q646E, P651K, L653V, I659L, T660A).
source: The remaining 11 individual residue substitutions we tested, which largely localize to positions in extracellular pore loops that are less conserved between TRPV channels (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), resulted in RTx-insensitive constructs that were still activated by 2-APB (L596V, L599F, S613K, D618P, S620E, I644F, Q646E, P651K, L653V, I659L, T660A; Figure 2B,C, grey).
evidence: Experimental results shown in Figure 2B,C and described in text.

claim: Only the side-chain of V587 is close enough to bound RTx to directly interact with the agonist.
source: Out of all substituted residues that conferred RTx responsiveness to TRPV3-6M, only the side-chain of V587 is close enough to the bound RTx to directly interact with the agonist, judging from the distances between bound RTx and side-chains from that equivalent position in the RTx/DkTx-bound TRPV1 structure (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) (Gao et al., 2016) or the RTx-bound TRPV2-4M structure (Zubcevic et al., 2018b).
evidence: Inference based on structural analysis of TRPV1 and TRPV2-4M structures with citations.

claim: WT TRPV3 failed to respond to a single heat stimulus <50°C.
source: For WT TRPV3, we failed to observe any response to a single heat stimulus <50°C, but observed robust responses to 2-APB (Figure 3C,F), consistent with previous reports (Liu et al., 2011; Liu and Qin, 2017).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 3C,F and described in text with citations to previous reports.

claim: WT TRPV3 exhibited robust responses to 2-APB.
source: For WT TRPV3, we failed to observe any response to a single heat stimulus <50°C, but observed robust responses to 2-APB (Figure 3C,F), consistent with previous reports (Liu et al., 2011; Liu and Qin, 2017).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 3C,F and described in text with citations to previous reports.

claim: TRPV3-6M did not respond to heat <50°C.
source: We observed the same result for TRPV3-6M, indicating that the 6M mutations do not noticeably influence channel activation or temperature-sensing (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and described in text.

claim: The 6M mutations do not noticeably influence TRPV3 channel activation or temperature-sensing.
source: We observed the same result for TRPV3-6M, indicating that the 6M mutations do not noticeably influence channel activation or temperature-sensing (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental result that TRPV3-6M behaved like WT TRPV3 in response to heat.

claim: Four out of five single point mutants (V587L, F625L, F656I and F666Y) displayed strong responses to 2-APB but no activation by temperatures below 50°C.
source: Four out of five single point mutants (V587L, F625L, F656I and F666Y) displayed strong responses to 2-APB but no activation by temperatures below 50°C (Figure 3F and Figure 31—figure supplement 1B–E), with a heat-sensitivity of current-temperature relations that was not qualitatively different from ion diffusion as assessed from their Q10 values (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Experimental results shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–E and described in text.

claim: The A606V mutant exhibited temperature-activated currents below 45°C.
source: In contrast, the A606V mutant exhibited temperature-activated currents below 45°C, which were clearly larger than the responses of WT TRPV3 and TRPV3-6M, but slightly smaller than those of TRPV1 in terms of Q10 and magnitude relative to 2-APB (Figure 3D,F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 3D,F and described in text.

claim: The A606V mutation facilitates TRPV3 activation through multiple modalities, including RTx and heat.
source: This result suggests that the mutation at A606 facilitates TRPV3 activation through multiple modalities, including RTx and heat.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental results showing A606V enables both RTx and heat activation.

claim: TRPV3-5PM construct exhibited responses to heat and Q10 values qualitatively similar to the A606V mutant.
source: We also found that the responses to heat and the associated Q10 values of the TRPV3/V2P chimera with and without the 6M mutations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2), and the TRPV3-5PM construct with all five cumulative pore mutations in the WT TRPV3 background (i.e. without the 6M mutations) (Figure 3E,F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2) were qualitatively similar to that of the A606V mutant.
evidence: Experimental results shown in Figure 3E,F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and described in text.

claim: The other four pore positions (V587L, F625L, F656I, F666Y) do not contribute to temperature-dependent activation.
source: These results suggest that the other four positions in the pore do not contribute to temperature-dependent activation.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental results showing these mutants did not respond to heat.

claim: TRPV3-4PM exhibited no response to temperatures below 50°C.
source: Consistently, a construct containing all pore mutations except A606V (TRPV3-4PM) exhibited no response to temperatures below 50°C (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H and described in text.

claim: The apparent affinity of WT TRPV3 for 2-APB is 460 ± 12 µM.
source: We first measured the response of WT TRPV3 to 2-APB, and obtained an apparent affinity of 460 ± 12 µM (Figure 4A,F), consistent with a previous report (Phelps et al., 2010).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 4A,F and described in text with citation to previous report.

claim: The V587L mutation did not have any effect on the apparent affinity for 2-APB (440 ± 13 µM).
source: Interestingly, the V587L mutation, which robustly promotes activation by RTx (Figure 2B), did not have any effect on the apparent affinity for 2-APB (440 ± 13 µM; Figure 4B,F).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 4B,F and described in text.

claim: The A606V mutation produced a ~3.5 fold increase in the apparent affinity for 2-APB to 132 ± 7 µM.
source: In contrast, the A606V mutation produced a detectable (~3.5 fold) increase in the apparent affinity to 132 ± 7 µM (Figure 4C,F), consistent with this mutation having a generalized effect on TRPV3 channel gating, as it affects the sensitivity of the channel to all tested stimuli.
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 4C,F and described in text.

claim: TRPV3-4PM exhibited a ~2 fold shift in the apparent affinity for 2-APB (210 ± 2 µM).
source: Interestingly, we found that a construct containing four cumulative pore mutations without A606V (TRPV3-4PM) exhibited a small ~2 fold shift in the apparent affinity for 2-APB (210 ± 2 µM, Figure 4D,F), which combined synergistically with A606V in TRPV3-5PM for a 20-fold increase in the apparent affinity (19 ± 2 µM, Figure 4E,F).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 4D,F and described in text.

claim: TRPV3-5PM exhibited a 20-fold increase in the apparent affinity for 2-APB (19 ± 2 µM).
source: Interestingly, we found that a construct containing four cumulative pore mutations without A606V (TRPV3-4PM) exhibited a small ~2 fold shift in the apparent affinity for 2-APB (210 ± 2 µM, Figure 4D,F), which combined synergistically with A606V in TRPV3-5PM for a 20-fold increase in the apparent affinity (19 ± 2 µM, Figure 4E,F).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 4E,F and described in text.

claim: The five residues in the pore facilitate opening by distinct mechanisms, differentially affecting activation by heat and 2-APB, while each enabling activation by RTx.
source: Together, these results suggest that the five residues in the pore facilitate opening by distinct mechanisms, differentially affecting activation by heat and 2-APB, while each enabling activation by RTx.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental results showing differential effects of mutations on different stimuli.

claim: Application of RTx together with heating resulted in prominent activation of TRPV3-6M at temperatures only slightly above room temperature.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, application of a short heating pulse together with RTx resulted in prominent activation of TRPV3-6M at temperatures only slightly above room temperature (Figure 5B), in contrast to the lack of response to heating up to 45°C in the absence of RTx for the same construct (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 5B and described in text.

claim: RTx and temperature act cooperatively to activate TRPV3-6M under conditions where neither stimulus alone would suffice.
source: These results indicate that RTx and temperature act cooperatively to activate TRPV3-6M under conditions where neither stimulus alone would suffice.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental result showing activation only when both RTx and heat are applied.

claim: Activation of the TRPV3-6M/V2P chimera to RTx at room temperature could be reduced to baseline levels when temperature was decreased to 10°C.
source: In addition, activation of the TRPV3-6M/V2P chimera to RTx observed at room temperature could be reduced to baseline levels when temperature was decreased to 10°C (Figure 5C), providing further evidence of coupling between heat-dependent activation and RTx sensitivity.
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 5C and described in text.

claim: Application of RTx after a short stimulation with 2-APB resulted in robust activation of TRPV3-6M channels in the absence of additional pore mutations.
source: Similar to our results with heat, application of RTx after a short stimulation with 2-APB did not activate WT TRPV3 channels (Figure 5D), but resulted in robust activation of TRPV3-6M channels in the absence of additional pore mutations (Figure 5E).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 5E and described in text.

claim: RTx binds to the TRPV3-6M channel, but further facilitation of channel opening is required for the vanilloid to activate TRPV3-6M.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that RTx binds to the TRPV3-6M channel, but that further facilitation of channel opening is required for the vanilloid to activate TRPV3-6M.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental results showing RTx activation requires additional stimuli or mutations.

claim: TRPV3 contains a 'defunct' vanilloid-binding site that can be made functional by mutating a few key positions in the binding pocket.
source: Our results demonstrate that like TRPV2, the TRPV3 channel contains a 'defunct' vanilloid-binding site that can be readily made functional by mutating a few key positions in the binding pocket.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The allosteric machinery required for coupling vanilloid-binding to pore-opening has remained functional through evolution in both TRPV2 and TRPV3 channels.
source: More importantly, our results show that the allosteric machinery required for coupling vanilloid-binding to pore-opening has remained functional through evolution in both TRPV2 and TRPV3 channels, even though these two channels are not naturally sensitive to vanilloid molecules.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Agonist sensitivity in TRP channels is fine-tuned by the structure of the agonist-binding pocket and by the intrinsic energetics of activation that are influenced by multiple sites throughout the pore.
source: This indicates that agonist sensitivity in TRP channels is not only fine-tuned by the structure of the agonist-binding pocket, but also by the intrinsic energetics of activation that are influenced by multiple sites throughout the pore.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: RTx-sensitive TRPV2 and TRPV3 constructs cannot be activated by capsaicin.
source: Indeed, RTx-sensitive TRPV2 and TRPV3 constructs cannot be activated by capsaicin (Yang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and data not shown), a vanilloid exhibiting much lower apparent affinity when compared to RTx.
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and described in text with citations.

claim: Capsaicin is a vanilloid exhibiting much lower apparent affinity when compared to RTx.
source: Indeed, RTx-sensitive TRPV2 and TRPV3 constructs cannot be activated by capsaicin (Yang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and data not shown), a vanilloid exhibiting much lower apparent affinity when compared to RTx.
evidence: Stated as known property of capsaicin.

claim: TRPV3-5PM channels cannot be activated by low pH.
source: Finally, the five identified pore mutations added cumulatively to TRPV3 did not have an effect on activation by other TRPV1-specific stimuli, such as extracellular protons (Jordt et al., 2000) or double knot toxin (DkTx) (Bohlen et al., 2010; Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C), consistent with the absence of binding sites for these two modulators in TRPV3.
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and described in text.

claim: TRPV3-5PM channels cannot be activated by double knot toxin (DkTx).
source: Finally, the five identified pore mutations added cumulatively to TRPV3 did not have an effect on activation by other TRPV1-specific stimuli, such as extracellular protons (Jordt et al., 2000) or double knot toxin (DkTx) (Bohlen et al., 2010; Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C), consistent with the absence of binding sites for these two modulators in TRPV3.
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and described in text.

claim: TRPV3 lacks binding sites for extracellular protons and double knot toxin.
source: Finally, the five identified pore mutations added cumulatively to TRPV3 did not have an effect on activation by other TRPV1-specific stimuli, such as extracellular protons (Jordt et al., 2000) or double knot toxin (DkTx) (Bohlen et al., 2010; Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C), consistent with the absence of binding sites for these two modulators in TRPV3.
evidence: Inference drawn from the lack of response to these stimuli.

claim: The vanilloid-binding pocket region is highly similar in TRPV1, TRPV2 and TRPV3 in terms of amino acid sequence conservation.
source: The vanilloid-binding pocket region is highly similar in TRPV1, TRPV2 and TRPV3, both in terms of amino acid sequence conservation (Figure 1A) and 3-dimensional structure (Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016; Huynh et al., 2016; Zubcevic et al., 2016; Singh et al., 2018; Zubcevic et al., 2018b) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and four mutations are sufficient to confer RTx sensitivity to the rat, mouse and rabbit TRPV2 channels (Yang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016; Zubcevic et al., 2018b).
evidence: Stated with reference to Figure 1A showing sequence alignment.

claim: The vanilloid-binding pocket region is highly similar in TRPV1, TRPV2 and TRPV3 in terms of 3-dimensional structure.
source: The vanilloid-binding pocket region is highly similar in TRPV1, TRPV2 and TRPV3, both in terms of amino acid sequence conservation (Figure 1A) and 3-dimensional structure (Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016; Huynh et al., 2016; Zubcevic et al., 2016; Singh et al., 2018; Zubcevic et al., 2018b) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and four mutations are sufficient to confer RTx sensitivity to the rat, mouse and rabbit TRPV2 channels (Yang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016; Zubcevic et al., 2018b).
evidence: Stated with citations to structural studies and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Four mutations are sufficient to confer RTx sensitivity to the rat, mouse and rabbit TRPV2 channels.
source: The vanilloid-binding pocket region is highly similar in TRPV1, TRPV2 and TRPV3, both in terms of amino acid sequence conservation (Figure 1A) and 3-dimensional structure (Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016; Huynh et al., 2016; Zubcevic et al., 2016; Singh et al., 2018; Zubcevic et al., 2018b) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and four mutations are sufficient to confer RTx sensitivity to the rat, mouse and rabbit TRPV2 channels (Yang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016; Zubcevic et al., 2018b).
evidence: Stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Most of the residues that enable RTx activation when mutated (V587, F625 and F656) are located at the protein/lipid interface, close to the RTx-binding pocket in TRPV1 and TRPV2-4M.
source: Most of these residues (V587, F625 and F656) are located at the protein/lipid interface, close to the RTx-binding pocket in TRPV1 and TRPV2-4M (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C) (Gao et al., 2016; Zubcevic et al., 2018b).
evidence: Stated with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C and citations to structural studies.

claim: A606 is tightly packed between the S5 helix and the pore helix of the same subunit.
source: A606 is tightly packed between the S5 helix and the pore helix of the same subunit (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Stated with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B showing structural location.

claim: F666 is facing the ion-conduction pathway and is located at a key position in the S6 helix proposed to function as a gating hinge in TRPV channels.
source: F666 is facing the ion-conduction pathway, and is located at a key position in the S6 helix proposed to function as a gating hinge in TRPV channels (Palovcak et al., 2015; Zubcevic et al., 2016; Kasimova et al., 2018; McGoldrick et al., 2018) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,D).
evidence: Stated with citations to previous work and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,D.

claim: State-dependent differences in the free energy contributions of individual side-chains throughout the protein can determine sensitivity to an agonist without requiring that each of these residues forms part of an interconnected allosteric network.
source: The observation that each of the 10 identified residues enable RTx activation when mutated individually, together with their wide-spread distribution within the pore domain, suggest that state-dependent differences in the free energy contributions of individual side-chains throughout the protein can determine sensitivity to an agonist without requiring that each of these residues forms part of an interconnected allosteric network.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental results showing individual mutations enable RTx activation.

claim: RTx is very hydrophobic and likely experiences pronounced membrane partitioning and accumulation.
source: However, RTx is very hydrophobic and likely experiences pronounced membrane partitioning and accumulation, which together with likely a high affinity for the TRPV3-6M channels results in an exceedingly slow dissociation as described previously for TRPV1 and TRPV2-4M (Yang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016), and as shown for TRPV3-6M + V587L and a construct containing all 5 cumulative pore mutations in the 6M background (TRPV3-6M + 5PM) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated with citations to previous work and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: RTx exhibits exceedingly slow dissociation from TRPV3-6M + V587L and TRPV3-6M + 5PM.
source: However, RTx is very hydrophobic and likely experiences pronounced membrane partitioning and accumulation, which together with likely a high affinity for the TRPV3-6M channels results in an exceedingly slow dissociation as described previously for TRPV1 and TRPV2-4M (Yang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016), and as shown for TRPV3-6M + V587L and a construct containing all 5 cumulative pore mutations in the 6M background (TRPV3-6M + 5PM) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and described in text.

claim: The TRPV3 channel can only initially be activated by heat at temperatures > 50°C, but will respond to much lower temperatures on subsequent heating.
source: For example, the TRPV3 channel can only initially be activated by heat at temperatures > 50°C, but will respond to much lower temperatures on subsequent heating (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated with citation to previous work.

claim: Activation of TRPV3 seems to involve a transition with a large energy barrier.
source: Before any previous stimulation, activation of TRPV3 seems to involve a transition with a large energy barrier, as either higher concentrations of 2-APB or temperatures > 50°C are initially required for robust activation when compared to subsequent stimulations, which elicit maximal activation at lower temperatures (<40°C) or 2-APB concentrations (Chung et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2011; Liu and Qin, 2017).
evidence: Stated with citations to previous work.

claim: TRPV3 'sensitization' is irreversible over the explored time-scale of several minutes.
source: This 'sensitization' is irreversible over the explored time-scale of several minutes, indicating that the return kinetic barrier towards the initial closed state is also high, and making it possible to shift the net apparent gating equilibrium towards the open state by either surpassing or reducing this kinetic barrier (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated with citation to previous work.

claim: Activation of TRPV1 and TRPV2 by heat involves significant hysteresis.
source: Activation of TRPV1 and TRPV2 by heat involves significant hysteresis as well, as both the apparent threshold for activation and the steepness of the current-temperature relations are reduced after channels have been initially activated by heat (Liu and Qin, 2016; Sánchez-Moreno et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated with citations to previous work.

claim: TRPV1 channel opening by capsaicin does not involve hysteresis.
source: However, in contrast to TRPV3, TRPV1 channel opening by the vanilloid capsaicin does not involve hysteresis (Liu and Qin, 2016), suggesting that TRPV1 activation by vanilloids does not necessarily require overcoming a large initial energy barrier.
evidence: Stated with citation to previous work.

claim: Initial activation of TRPV1 and TRPV2 with 2-APB sensitizes both channels to subsequent 2-APB applications.
source: Furthermore, initial activation of TRPV1 and TRPV2 with 2-APB sensitizes both channels to subsequent 2-APB applications (Liu and Qin, 2016), but to a lesser degree than in TRPV3 (Chung et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2011) and more importantly, without influencing the apparent threshold or sensitivity to activation by heat (Liu and Qin, 2016).
evidence: Stated with citations to previous work.

claim: A large energy barrier is an obligatory component of activation for TRPV3.
source: Together, these observations raise the possibility that a large energy barrier is an obligatory component of activation for TRPV3, whereas activation of TRPV1 and TRPV2 by some stimuli follows a path that does not involve a large kinetic barrier.
evidence: Inference drawn from comparing activation properties of TRPV1, TRPV2, and TRPV3.

claim: Activation of TRPV1 and TRPV2 by some stimuli follows a path that does not involve a large kinetic barrier.
source: Together, these observations raise the possibility that a large energy barrier is an obligatory component of activation for TRPV3, whereas activation of TRPV1 and TRPV2 by some stimuli follows a path that does not involve a large kinetic barrier.
evidence: Inference drawn from comparing activation properties of TRPV1, TRPV2, and TRPV3.

claim: The open and closed TRPV3 structures exhibit far more drastic differences than those of open and closed TRPV1 and TRPV6 structures.
source: The structural origin of this kinetic barrier is not known, but it is interesting to note that the open and closed TRPV3 structures exhibit far more drastic differences than those of open and closed TRPV1 (Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016) and TRPV6 (McGoldrick et al., 2018) structures, including significant changes in the length of the S6 and TRP helices, and a 20° rotation of the rest of the channel relative to the pore domain (Singh et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated with citations to structural studies.

claim: The α- to π-transition in the S6 helix observed between the human apo and the 2-APB-sensitized TRPV3 structures may be part of the sensitization mechanism in TRPV3.
source: Based in these structures it was suggested that the α- to π-transition in the S6 helix observed between the human apo and the 2-APB-sensitized structures may be part of the sensitization mechanism in TRPV3 (Zubcevic et al., 2018a), as no such transition has been structurally observed for TRPV1 or TRPV2 (see discussion above).
evidence: Stated with citation to previous work.

claim: RTx binding to TRPV3-6M channels is not sufficient to overcome the large energy barrier for activation.
source: It is therefore possible that RTx binding to TRPV3-6M channels is not sufficient to overcome this large energy barrier, either because the vanilloid site in TRPV3-6M may lack the allosteric connections to influence this slow transition, or because of energetically weaker coupling of the RTx site to the gating machinery.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental results and structural considerations.

claim: The vanilloid site in TRPV3-6M may lack the allosteric connections to influence the slow transition associated with the large energy barrier.
source: It is therefore possible that RTx binding to TRPV3-6M channels is not sufficient to overcome this large energy barrier, either because the vanilloid site in TRPV3-6M may lack the allosteric connections to influence this slow transition, or because of energetically weaker coupling of the RTx site to the gating machinery.
evidence: Speculation based on the experimental results.

claim: The binding of RTx to TRPV3-6M and TRPV2-4M and/or its coupling to the pore might not function as efficiently as in TRPV1.
source: It is likely that the binding of RTx to TRPV3-6M and TRPV2-4M and/or its coupling to the pore might not function as efficiently as in TRPV1.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The A606V mutation facilitates activation by all tested stimuli.
source: The A606V mutation facilitates activation by all tested stimuli, suggesting that it has a global effect on gating, possibly by favoring activation of the heat-sensing machinery, enhancing the efficacy of coupling between the stimulus-sensing domains and the pore, directly reducing the large kinetic barrier in the activation pathway and/or directly stabilizing the open state.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental results showing A606V affects multiple stimuli.

claim: Residue A606 at the top of the S5 helix is tightly packed against the pore helix of the same subunit.
source: Structurally, residue A606 at the top of the S5 helix is tightly packed against the pore helix of the same subunit (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B), so that the A606V mutation might influence the relative positioning of these two helices, resulting in a global effect on gating.
evidence: Stated with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B showing structural location.

claim: The A606V mutation might influence the relative positioning of the S5 helix and pore helix, resulting in a global effect on gating.
source: Structurally, residue A606 at the top of the S5 helix is tightly packed against the pore helix of the same subunit (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B), so that the A606V mutation might influence the relative positioning of these two helices, resulting in a global effect on gating.
evidence: Speculation based on structural considerations.

claim: V587 is located at a critical junction between the S4-S5 linker- and S5-helices that undergoes an α to π transition between the apo-TRPV2 and RTx-bound TRPV2-4M structures.
source: Importantly, V587 is located at a critical junction between the S4-S5 linker- and S5-helices that undergoes an α to π transition between the apo-TRPV2 and RTx-bound TRPV2-4M structures (Zubcevic et al., 2018b).
evidence: Stated with citation to structural study.

claim: The α to π transition at the S4-S5 linker/S5 junction appears to be fundamental for coupling RTx-binding to gating in TRPV2-4M.
source: This transition appears to be fundamental for coupling RTx-binding to gating in this channel, which is consistent with a key role of the S4-S5 linker in transducing the binding of capsaicin or RTx to the opening of the pore proposed for TRPV1 based on structural (Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016) and functional data (Yang et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated with citations to structural and functional studies.

claim: V587L specifically enhances the coupling between RTx binding and gating by influencing the conformational dynamics of the S4-S5 linker helix.
source: It is therefore possible that V587L specifically enhances the coupling between RTx binding and gating by influencing the conformational dynamics of the S4-S5 linker helix.
evidence: Speculation based on structural considerations and experimental results.

claim: Multiple non-protein densities observed at the protein/membrane interface in the apo- or RTx/DkTx-bound structures of TRPV1 in nanodiscs have been proposed to correspond to bound lipids.
source: Multiple non-protein densities observed at that interface in the apo- or RTx/DkTx-bound structures of TRPV1 in nanodiscs have been proposed to correspond to bound lipids (Gao et al., 2016), which take different positions in the two structures and suggest gating-associated lipid rearrangements (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Stated with citation to structural study and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Activation of TRPV3 by 2-APB involves the expulsion of a lipid bound near side chain Y650.
source: For TRPV3 it was suggested that activation by 2-APB involves the expulsion of a lipid bound near side chain Y650, based on a non-protein density close to Y650 in the apo structure of mouse TRPV3 that is absent in the 2-APB-bound open structure (Singh et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated with citation to structural study.

claim: Channel-lipid interactions at the protein/membrane interface could play a role in channel activation by RTx.
source: Channel-lipid interactions at that interface could play a role in channel activation by RTx, raising the possibility that mutations in that interface that enable RTx activation of TRPV3-6M do so by altering protein-lipid interactions.
evidence: Speculation based on structural observations and experimental results.

claim: The equivalent residue Y671 in TRPV1 has been proposed to be responsible for coupling capsaicin-induced conformational changes in S6 to the selectivity filter and pore-helices.
source: The equivalent residue Y671 in TRPV1 has been proposed to be responsible for coupling capsaicin-induced conformational changes in S6 to the selectivity filter and pore-helices (Palovcak et al., 2015; Kasimova et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated with citations to previous work.

claim: F666Y has a similar role in activation of TRPV3-6M by RTx as Y671 in TRPV1 activation by capsaicin.
source: It is therefore possible that F666Y has a similar role in activation of TRPV3-6M by RTx, while activation by 2-APB and temperature could engage other mechanisms to influence the conformation of the filter and pore-helices.
evidence: Speculation based on comparison with TRPV1.

claim: Conformational changes in the pore-helix and selectivity filter are important in the late stages of the mechanism of TRPV1 activation by capsaicin.
source: L635F and L639M also enable weak responses to RTx, and are in the pore-helix or selectivity filter, respectively, consistent with the hypothesis that conformational changes in those regions are important in the late stages of the mechanism of TRPV1 activation by capsaicin (Kasimova et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Phe to Leu substitutions at equivalent positions in TRPV1 (F640L) or TRPV2 (F603L) result in potentiated responses to heat or 2-APB, respectively, and higher basal channel activity.
source: However, contrary to the stimulating effect of the L635F mutation in TRPV3-6M, Phe to Leu substitutions at equivalent positions in TRPV1 (F640L) or TRPV2 (F603L) also result in potentiated responses to heat or 2-APB, respectively, and higher basal channel activity (Myers et al., 2008).
evidence: Stated with citation to previous work.

claim: The five identified pore mutations added cumulatively to TRPV3 did not have an effect on activation by extracellular protons.
source: Finally, the five identified pore mutations added cumulatively to TRPV3 did not have an effect on activation by other TRPV1-specific stimuli, such as extracellular protons (Jordt et al., 2000) or double knot toxin (DkTx) (Bohlen et al., 2010; Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C), consistent with the absence of binding sites for these two modulators in TRPV3.
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and described in text.

claim: The five identified pore mutations added cumulatively to TRPV3 did not have an effect on activation by double knot toxin (DkTx).
source: Finally, the five identified pore mutations added cumulatively to TRPV3 did not have an effect on activation by other TRPV1-specific stimuli, such as extracellular protons (Jordt et al., 2000) or double knot toxin (DkTx) (Bohlen et al., 2010; Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C), consistent with the absence of binding sites for these two modulators in TRPV3.
evidence: Experimental result shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and described in text.

claim: Conservative side-chain modifications, such as V587L or I595L, can have a dramatic effect on the response to RTx in TRPV3-6M.
source: The fact that conservative side-chain modifications, such as V587L or I595L, can have such a dramatic effect on the response to RTx in TRPV3-6M raises the possibility that other relatively subtle structural alterations, such as those caused by the binding of another ligand, a post-translational modification, or an alteration in the properties of the membrane, could enable responses to channel modulators that would otherwise seem inactive.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Subtle structural alterations, such as those caused by the binding of another ligand, a post-translational modification, or an alteration in the properties of the membrane, could enable responses to channel modulators that would otherwise seem inactive.
source: The fact that conservative side-chain modifications, such as V587L or I595L, can have such a dramatic effect on the response to RTx in TRPV3-6M raises the possibility that other relatively subtle structural alterations, such as those caused by the binding of another ligand, a post-translational modification, or an alteration in the properties of the membrane, could enable responses to channel modulators that would otherwise seem inactive.
evidence: Speculation based on the experimental results.

claim: Fine structural differences dictate the response of a TRPV channel to an agonist or combination of agonists.
source: The picture of TRPV channel gating that emerges from this study is one where fine structural differences dictate the response of a channel to an agonist or combination of agonists.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Understanding fine structural differences might be key to unraveling the mechanisms of allosteric signal integration in TRP channels.
source: Understanding these differences might be key to unraveling the mechanisms of allosteric signal integration in TRP channels.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.
